quote.translation: When Plato, for example, speaks of "by chance (τύχη), out of necessity (ἀνάγκη)" (Platon, Leges, X, 889), when Leibniz speaks of "trying to attribute everything to the necessity of matter or to some chance" (Leibniz, Discours de métaphysique, § 19), and when Engels speaks of "the necessity immanent in chance" (Dialectics of Nature, vol. 2, Iwanami Bunko, p. 28), they refer to the combination of causal necessity and teleological contingency.

regions.text: トーマスの謂はゆる「必然性または偶然性の法則」（lexnecessitatisvelcontingentiac）は自由としての因果的偶然性と据理としての目々必然性との結合を提唱してゐるものである。

quote.translation: Thomas's so-called "law of necessity or contingency" (lex necessitatis vel contingentiae) advocates the combination of causal contingency as freedom with teleological necessity as providence.

regions.text: またラングが「唯物論史」のうちで「偶然と必然ほと完全に相矛盾するものは他にない。それにも拘らす、雨者ほと屢々混同されるものも他にない」（Lange,GeschichtedesMaterialismus,1S13）と云ってゐるのも、一方に因果必然性と目々偶然性他方に目々必然性と因果偶然

quote.translation: And when Lange writes in his History of Materialism that "no two things contradict each other so completely as chance and necessity, and nevertheless there is nothing else that is so often confused as the two" (Lange, Geschichte des Materialismus, I. S. 13), this too is because the combination of causal necessity with teleological contingency on the one side, and of teleological necessity with causal contingency on the other, so readily comes about.
